t: Scurvy, measles, sickle-cell and lung cancer are all illnesses. Not one of them is caused the same way as another.

Four diseases, four completely different kinds of cause: something missing, something caught, something inherited, and something breathed in. Treating them as one category is why medicine took so long to work.
sub: So 'illness' is not one kind of thing.
Working out which kind you are looking at is most of a diagnosis.

label: Something outside did damage
Environmental: an external agent causing damage

t: Illnesses come in kinds, and the kind tells you what might help.
Infectious, deficiency, genetic, environmental and degenerative — five broad categories, and the category determines what kind of intervention could possibly work.

The categories overlap: most common diseases have genetic susceptibility interacting with environmental exposure, and infection can be a cause of cancer. The classification is a starting point rather than a partition.

Germ theory's great achievement was separating the first category out, and its great distortion was that for fifty years afterwards people looked for a germ behind everything. Scurvy was thought infectious. So was pellagra, and Goldberger had to drink a patient's excretions to convince anyone otherwise — the categories are not obvious from the outside.
sub: An antibiotic helps with exactly one of these, and does nothing for the rest.
That is worth stating plainly: antibiotics work on bacterial infection only, and not on viruses, deficiencies, inherited conditions or damage.
Which is why they are prescribed so often for things they cannot touch, and why that drives resistance for no benefit at all.

Roughly a third of antibiotic prescriptions in primary care are for conditions they cannot help — mostly viral. The cost is not merely waste: every prescription applies selection pressure, so a drug given for no benefit still buys resistance.

q: Will an antibiotic help a cold?
Are antibiotics effective against viral infections?
Why does prescribing an antibiotic for a virus have a cost rather than merely no benefit?
options: No — a cold is a virus, and antibiotics only work on bacteria
Only if you take it early enough
why: Antibiotics attack things bacteria have and viruses do not — like their cell walls. A virus has none of those, so there is nothing for the drug to attack.
They target bacterial structures and processes that viruses do not possess. There is no mechanism by which one could act on a virus, so timing makes no difference either.

Because the selection pressure is applied regardless of whether the drug helps. The bacteria in and on the patient are exposed, resistant ones survive, and resistance accumulates — so an ineffective prescription is not neutral, it spends a shared resource for nothing. That is the same mechanism you ran in the beetle simulation.

t: Working out what kind of thing you are dealing with is the first half of solving it.

The category determines what could possibly work: replace what is missing, kill what got in, manage what was inherited, remove what is doing damage. Most diagnostic error is not getting the specific disease wrong — it is being in the wrong category, and then every subsequent step is wasted however well executed.
